card.hook: The Promenade is about 7 kilometres long, so trying to fit it into one photo is a bit like squeezing a sofa into a lift. The trick is to stop trying and let one blue chair do the talking.
card.stand_here: Stand in Jardin Albert Ier at the blue chairs between the garden and the Musée Masséna, and face the sea. The subject is about 1.8 km to the west along the Promenade, so let it stretch away to your left-hand side of the bay.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get a blue chair and the palm trees close in, then switch to 1x for a calmer, more natural view of the bay. If your phone has 2x or 5x, try those to pull the curve of the coast closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on a line so the sea sits level, then crouch a little and place a blue chair low in the foreground.
card.best_time: Early morning or around sunset, when the light is softer. It's a good spot for sunrise too.
card.selfie_here: For the classic one, head to the #ILoveNice letters on the Quai Rauba Capéu pier at the far end of the Promenade and pose in front of them with the sea behind you. For something more playful, squeeze in beside the giant tilted blue chair (La Chaise Bleue de SAB) on the seafront. Use the front camera, or 0.5x to fit more in, and check the sign and chair are still in place before you go.
card.ask_someone: At the Colline du Château viewpoint you can see the whole Promenade and the bay below, so it's a nice place to ask someone to take your photo with the view behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The Promenade is an open public walkway and the blue-chair viewpoint is free. If you plan to visit Castle Hill, check its opening hours first, especially for evening light.
card.challenge: Take three frames: a blue chair close up with the bay behind, a wider one with the palms, and one with the Promenade curving away. Then pick your favourite.
card.good_to_know: The Promenade began in the 1820s as a path paid for by the Reverend Lewis Way and members of the English church in Nice. It's named after those English winter visitors, and locals simply call it 'La Prom'. It also finished the 2024 Tour de France.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Jardin Albert Ier at the blue chairs between the garden and the Musée Masséna, and face the sea. The subject is about 1.8 km to the west along the Promenade, so let it stretch away to your left-hand side of the bay.

card.hook: Here's a fun puzzle for your camera roll: one frame, two centuries of building. The old villa and its newer wing sit side by side, and the Musée Matisse in Nice's Cimiez district shows off both.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Musée Matisse, right where the phone icon sits on the map, and face the front of the Villa des Arènes. If the whole front won't fit, take a step or two back as the surroundings allow, then check that the walls aren't cut off at the edges of your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole front of the villa. Use 0.5x only if you're very close and can't fit it in, and keep the villa in the middle so the edges don't stretch. Then try zoom 2x for windows and stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and line up the villa's vertical edges with them so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light flatters a building front and avoids harsh midday shadows. If the sky is bright, tap the wall and drag it a little darker so the villa doesn't go gloomy.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the olive-grove lawn in front of the museum, with the villa behind you and the olive grove and Roman ruins in view. Use the front camera and hold it a little low, so the coral facade with its sea-foam shutters fills the background over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the Parvis des Orangers, the open forecourt on the north side where both the villa and the modern wing show, while you pose in front of the building. There's no exact spot, so try a couple of positions when you get there.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are for personal use only, and flash isn't allowed because it damages the artworks. A tourism guide says selfie sticks are banned, but it doesn't say if that covers the grounds, so just hold your phone. Check the official site for photography rules before you go inside.
card.challenge: Take three frames: the whole villa, a doorway or window up close, and the spot where old villa meets new wing. Then pick your favourite.
card.good_to_know: The villa was built between 1670 and 1685. The museum opened in 1963 and reopened in 1993 after four years of renovation, when the modern wing was added. Matisse lived and worked in Nice from 1917 to 1954, and this is one of the largest collections of his work anywhere.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Musée Matisse, right where the phone icon sits on the map, and face the front of the Villa des Arènes. If the whole front won't fit, take a step or two back as the surroundings allow, then check that the walls aren't cut off at the edges of your screen.

card.hook: Most museums ask you to look at the art indoors. Here, Chagall left a mosaic outside for you, sitting above a calm pond, so you can start snapping before you even buy a ticket.
card.stand_here: Head for the Musée Marc Chagall itself. The phone icon on the map sits right at the museum, so there's no extra walk once you arrive. Once you're in the grounds, face the pond with the mosaic above it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the building and garden. Switch to 0.5x to squeeze the pond and mosaic into one frame, and keep your phone level so the walls don't lean. Then go to zoom 2x (or higher if your phone has it) for a close-up of the mosaic's colours.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the mosaic, then slide the brightness down a touch to make it darker if the sky is bright, so the colours stay rich.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light on the colours and less glare on the water. Midday sun can be harsh on the bright facade.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the edge of the outdoor pool next to the museum building, with the building behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the building over your shoulder. For a leafier shot, try one of the garden paths where the building peeks through the greenery.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pool's far edge, across from the museum, facing you, while you stand by the building, so the building and the pool both fit in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Non-flash photos for personal use in the permanent collection are generally allowed, but check signs or ask staff, as rules can change for temporary exhibitions. Flash is usually off-limits for the Biblical Message paintings. Access may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the mosaic's colours in the pool and catch them in one shot, with a little water in the foreground.
card.good_to_know: The museum opened in 1973 while Chagall was still alive, and he had a hand in how it was arranged. It was built around seventeen paintings illustrating the biblical message, which he gave to the French State in 1966. Chagall also made the mosaic over the pond and the blue stained glass windows in the concert hall, and he gave detailed instructions for the garden, which Henri Fish created.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the Musée Marc Chagall itself. The phone icon on the map sits right at the museum, so there's no extra walk once you arrive. Once you're in the grounds, face the pond with the mosaic above it.

card.hook: Here's a plot twist: there's no castle on Castle Hill. Louis XIV had it knocked down in 1706, and what's left is a park with one of the best views in Nice.
card.stand_here: Head to the Tour Bellanda roof terrace, on the southern edge of the hill. Face the bay, so the Baie des Anges curves away in front of you and the main part of the hill sits behind you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole sweep of the bay and the rooftops in one frame. Then try 1x for a calmer, more natural view, and 2x or 5x (if your phone has them) to pick out individual rooftops or boats.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line instead of the middle, with a strip of park trees or the terrace edge at the bottom for depth.
card.best_time: The views are good from sunrise to sundown. The main terraces get busy at sunset, so arrive early if you want a clear frame, and check the official site for opening hours before you go.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the Bellanda Tower roof terrace, with the bay in front of you and the hill rising behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a little high so the hill and the view both fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For a photo of you, ask a passer-by on Quai Rauba-Capeù, on the Port Lympia side of the promenade, to shoot you with the hill rising behind you (check the exact spot on the map).
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official site for the Tour Bellanda's opening hours and entry rules. Sources disagree on whether access is free or the lift costs a small fee, so check when you arrive.
card.challenge: Get the whole curve of the bay in one shot, with the horizon on a gridline and a little tree or terrace edge at the bottom. Then see if you can spot the Old Town's terracotta rooftops at 2x.
card.good_to_know: Castle Hill is about 93 metres high. A fortress stood here from the 11th to the 18th century and was besieged several times, including in 1543 and 1691. French troops took it in 1705, and it was destroyed in 1706 on Louis XIV's orders. That's why you find a garden and viewpoints instead of a castle.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the Tour Bellanda roof terrace, on the southern edge of the hill. Face the bay, so the Baie des Anges curves away in front of you and the main part of the hill sits behind you.

card.hook: Picture a whole postcard in one go: yachts bobbing at the bottom, pastel buildings in the middle, and Mont Boron rising up behind them. Nice's port packs it all into one frame, and the trick is to look down on it.
card.stand_here: Go to the southernmost point of Colline du Château, the hilltop park, and face the harbour. Port Lympia is right below you and Mont Boron fills the view across the water.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the harbour as you see it, then try 0.5x to squeeze in more port and hillside. For a closer shot of the yachts or the pastel buildings, use 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the line of the quay on the lower third, so the boats fill the bottom and Mont Boron fills the top.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the buildings and water than the middle of the day. Check how the light falls when you arrive.
card.selfie_here: Try the Phare de Nice, the lighthouse at the entrance of Port Lympia. A travel blog calls it a lesser-known photo spot with views of both the city and the port, so the harbour can sit behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and hold your phone a little higher so the lighthouse and port fit over your shoulder. Le Plongeoir, on the cliff edge between Coco Beach and Port Lympia, is another popular photo spot.
card.ask_someone: At the port-side lookout on the hilltop, next to the playground, stand at the railing with the harbour below you and ask a passer-by to step back and take your photo.
card.rules_and_safety: Take care with your footing and hold your phone securely with both hands. Check the official site for lift times and any closures before you go.
card.challenge: Get a yacht, a pastel building and Mont Boron all in one shot, then take a second one with just the boats and façades.
card.good_to_know: The Port of Nice is also called Port Lympia. Colline du Château is a free park, and you can get up by lift (at 1 Rue des Ponchettes) or by the stairs. For a different angle, Quai Lunel gives a wide view at water level, and Quai des Deux Emmanuel is good for closer shots of the traditional pointu boats.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go to the southernmost point of Colline du Château, the hilltop park, and face the harbour. Port Lympia is right below you and Mont Boron fills the view across the water.

card.hook: Nice has a giant checkerboard for a living room, and everyone ends up standing in it. The black-and-white paving does half your composing for you.
card.stand_here: Stand in Place Masséna on the tram-line side of the square. Face across the checkerboard paving towards the Fountain of the Sun, with the red arcaded buildings behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the checkerboard, the fountain and the buildings in one frame. Switch to 1x for a calmer, more natural view. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single statue or the fountain details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, hold the phone low and level, and line up the paving so the squares run straight towards the fountain.
card.best_time: Early morning or after dark is best. Tour groups fill the square during the day, and at night the statues and fountains are lit.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the Fountain of the Sun in the middle of the square, with the red-fronted buildings behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and keep the fountain over your shoulder. It's the square's favourite photo backdrop, so you'll be in good company.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an open public square, pedestrianised and open at all hours. Part of Jardin Albert 1er may be closed, so check locally before you go.
card.challenge: Find the seven kneeling statues on their tall poles along the tram line, and get one of them floating in the sky above the checkerboard.
card.good_to_know: The square was laid out by Joseph Vernier in 1843-1844 and is named after André Masséna. It's roughly 260 metres across, so there's plenty of room to step back. The kneeling figures are Jaume Plensa's 2007 work 'Conversation in Nice'.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Place Masséna on the tram-line side of the square. Face across the checkerboard paving towards the Fountain of the Sun, with the red arcaded buildings behind it.

card.hook: Picture a street so full of awnings and stalls that the middle of it is basically a patchwork quilt. That's Cours Saleya in the morning, and the trick is to see it from the quiet end.
card.stand_here: Go to Place Charles Félix at the eastern end of the cours, next to the Palais Caïs de Pierlas, with Castle Hill rising behind you. The market lies about 260 m to the west, so face west and let the cours open out in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole view along the cours. Try zoom 2x to pull the far-off stalls closer, or zoom 0.5x if you want the square and the palace in the frame too (zoom levels depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the middle of the cours down the centre of the frame, and let the rows of awnings lead the eye in.
card.best_time: Go in the morning while the market is running, when the street is at its most colourful and lively. On Mondays the flower market gives way to an antiques market, so the scene looks different.
card.selfie_here: Grab a seat on one of the café terraces along the cours, or step to the edge of the cours rather than the middle. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x, with the market and its awnings behind your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The cours and Place Charles Félix are open public spaces. If you plan to go up to Parc du Château, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap in the crowd and see if you can get the whole row of awnings leading straight to the middle of your shot, with no one's head in the way.
card.good_to_know: Cours Saleya is the long market street in the old town of Nice. For a higher view, Parc du Château looks down over the awnings and old town rooftops to the sea. The Escaliers des Ponchettes are a short climb too, but crowds and awnings partly block the view from there.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go to Place Charles Félix at the eastern end of the cours, next to the Palais Caïs de Pierlas, with Castle Hill rising behind you. The market lies about 260 m to the west, so face west and let the cours open out in front of you.

card.hook: Picture a giant pink-and-white wedding cake with a dome on top, parked next to a palm-lined boulevard. That's the Negresco, and guides call it the most photographed view from the Promenade des Anglais.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Promenade des Anglais, opposite the hotel facade and across the road from the Negresco. The hotel is to the north of you, so face north with the sea at your back.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the facade and dome together. If the whole building won't fit, tap 0.5x, but keep it away from the corners because they stretch. For a tighter shot of the dome, try 2x (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, hold your phone level, put the dome on the top line and let a palm lean in at the edge. Then tap the pink facade and drag the brighter/darker slider down a touch so the sky stays blue.
card.best_time: Early morning is best. The road is quiet, so you get fewer cars and people wandering through your frame.
card.selfie_here: Use the seafront pavement right in front of the hotel's pink dome. Switch to the front camera, try 0.5x, and tilt so the dome peeks over your shoulder. Bloggers call this a top Instagram backdrop.
card.ask_someone: For a calmer spot, try the Jardins du Musée Masséna right next to the Negresco and ask someone to take your photo there, away from the busy promenade.
card.rules_and_safety: The promenade is one of Nice's busiest streets, so wait for a clear gap before you step back for a shot, and never step into the road for the framing. The hotel is a private business, and one visitor was asked not to take photos inside because of other guests, so stick to the outside.
card.challenge: Get the dome on the top gridline with exactly two palms leaning in, and no car in the picture. Give yourself five tries.
card.good_to_know: Henri Negresco opened the hotel in 1912 and hired architect Édouard-Jean Niermans to design it, dome included. It served as a hospital in the First World War and was listed as a National Historic Building in 2003. The doormen still wear 18th-century-style costume with red-plumed hats.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Promenade des Anglais, opposite the hotel facade and across the road from the Negresco. The hotel is to the north of you, so face north with the sea at your back.

card.hook: Here's a confession: the best Promenade du Paillon photo starts in a square, not in the park. Red façades, checkerboard paving and a wall of green at the end make a fun, graphic shot, and it's a nice change from the usual water pictures.
card.stand_here: Stand in Place Masséna, with the Promenade du Paillon about 129 m to the north-east. Face that way, so the red buildings sit on both sides and the paving leads your eye towards the greenery.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the park entrance framed by the façades. Go to 0.5x if you want more of the checkerboard paving in the foreground, or 2x to pick out the greenery in the distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the paving up so it leads straight towards the park, with the red buildings balanced on each side.
card.best_time: Golden hour is when the red buildings look their best. The water jets are seasonal and may be off in cooler months, so check before you go if the water mirror is on your list.
card.selfie_here: Head into the park to the Place Masséna end of the reflecting pool (the water mirror) and stand with the pool behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a little low so the water and the park fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand along the edge of the reflecting pool, where a wide shot can take in the whole park, while you pose with the water mirror behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Be mindful of other visitors and keep your belongings secure around the water features. Check the official site before you go, especially for the water jets.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the paving lines point straight at the greenery, with a few people strolling along them so nobody gets cut off at the edges.
card.good_to_know: The Promenade du Paillon is a green park in Nice that begins at Place Masséna. The Miroir d'eau is its long water mirror, with jets in the foreground and the paths and buildings reflected in the water. Colline du Château gives a wide view over the rooftops, but it isn't part of the park and it's a walk uphill, so treat it as a separate outing.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Place Masséna, with the Promenade du Paillon about 129 m to the north-east. Face that way, so the red buildings sit on both sides and the paving leads your eye towards the greenery.

card.hook: Look up from the pavement and you'll spot statues lined up on the roof terrace, like they're waiting for the curtain to go up. This is the Opéra de Nice's full Belle Époque front, and it's a show all by itself.
card.stand_here: Stand on Rue Saint-François-de-Paule, directly opposite the main façade, and face the ceremonial entrance. From there you can fit the whole front into one frame, with the statues above the door.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole façade in. If the street is too narrow, drop to 0.5x, but keep the building away from the edges of the frame, where it can look stretched. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to home in on the statues and the carved detail.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, line the entrance up with the centre of the frame, and keep your phone level so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Crowds and light can vary, so check how busy it is when you arrive. If the sky is very bright, tap the façade and drag the brightness down a little so the stonework keeps its detail. If the light is low, use night mode and hold your phone steady against something solid.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the pavement facing the main façade on Rue Saint-François-de-Paule, under the four Muse statues on the roof. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if you want more building, and keep the opera over your shoulder. For a different backdrop, Quai des États-Unis works too, though that side is plainer.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally fine from public areas outside, but not during performances, so be discreet if an event is on. Check the official site for any works around the building before you go.
card.challenge: Get the entire front and the rooftop statues in one frame, then zoom in and see if you can pick out a statue's pose.
card.good_to_know: The first small wooden theatre on this site dates from 1776. A gas leak started a huge fire during a performance in March 1881 and destroyed the building. The city rebuilt it to designs by François Aune, and the new house opened in February 1885 with Verdi's Aida. It was named the Opéra de Nice in 1902.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Rue Saint-François-de-Paule, directly opposite the main façade, and face the ceremonial entrance. From there you can fit the whole front into one frame, with the statues above the door.

card.hook: Picture a clean, pale, perfectly symmetrical front standing against blue sky, with palm trees lined up in front like they've been told to behave. That's the Palais de la Méditerranée, and it makes you look like a better photographer than you are.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Promenade des Anglais, on the south side of the street, directly across from the facade (13-17 Promenade des Anglais). Face north-north-west toward the building. Use a pedestrian crossing to get there.
card.zoom: Zoom 0.5x fits the whole facade in one frame from across the road. Zoom 1x stretches the edges less. Then try zoom 2x to 5x for the carved reliefs and sea-horse figures.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the white columns with the vertical lines, then tap the facade and make it a touch darker so the stonework keeps its detail against the bright sky.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into early evening gives good light on the facade. Early morning means fewer people on the pavement.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a little low and out to the side. That way the pale facade fits over your shoulder and doesn't get hidden behind your head.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by on the sea side of the Promenade, opposite the facade, and ask them to frame the full front with you in the foreground.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the public pavement for exterior shots and use the pedestrian crossings rather than stepping into the traffic. Photos are fine outside, but not inside the casino, and rules can change in private venues, so ask staff before shooting indoors.
card.challenge: Walk a few steps along the pavement and find a sea-horse figure, then zoom in and see if you can get it looking back at you.
card.good_to_know: The Palais was built in 1928-29 by the architects Charles and Marcel Dalmas for the American millionaire Frank Jay Gould. It opened as a place of glamour, with a casino, theatre, restaurant and cocktail bar. Most of the old building was pulled down in 1990, but the main facade and the Rue du Congrès facade were kept as classified historical monuments. A nine-floor hotel and a casino now sit behind them.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Promenade des Anglais, on the south side of the street, directly across from the facade (13-17 Promenade des Anglais). Face north-north-west toward the building. Use a pedestrian crossing to get there.

card.hook: Up close, Nice Cathedral's front door is rather modest, and people often walk straight past it. Step back into the square and the whole thing finally makes sense.
card.stand_here: Stand in the middle of Place Rossetti, in front of the facade. The cathedral is 44 m west of you on the west side of the square, so face west.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole front and the tiled dome in one shot. Go to 2x for the dome and bell tower details, and use 0.5x only if the square is too crowded to step back.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the facade, then drag the slider a little darker so the facade and the sky both keep their detail.
card.best_time: Try early in the morning, when the square is usually quieter. When you arrive, check how the light falls on the facade before you pick your spot.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the middle of Place Rossetti and turn your back to the cathedral, so the facade and dome are behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and check the framing on screen before you smile.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand by the obelisk fountain on Place Rossetti and shoot toward the cathedral while you stand in front of the facade.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is open to everyone, but access and photos inside the cathedral can be limited during Mass and services, so check the official site first. Inside, skip the flash and respect any services.
card.challenge: Take three frames with different amounts of square in them, then pick the one where the fountain isn't blocking the door.
card.good_to_know: The main body was built between 1650 and 1685 and consecrated in 1699. The facade you see today dates from 1825 to 1830, and the dome is covered in coloured glazed tiles in the Genoese style. The cathedral has been a national monument since 1906 and a minor basilica since 1949.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the middle of Place Rossetti, in front of the facade. The cathedral is 44 m west of you on the west side of the square, so face west.

card.hook: There's a stone cannonball stuck in a wall in Nice's old town, and it's been there since a siege in 1543. Put it in front of a glowing palace and you've got a night photo with a story.
card.stand_here: Stand on Rue de la Loge at the corner on the palace's edge, where the cannonball is set into the stonework. Face the lit-up palace, which you'll see at an angle.
card.zoom: Stay at 1x for the night view with the cannonball in front. On Rue Droite, where you can't step back, switch to 0.5x.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the walls upright, then tap the palace and slide it a little darker so the lit stonework doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go at night, when the palace is lit up. Rue Droite is the one to pick if you're here by day.
card.selfie_here: Try the Rue de la Loge corner by the cannonball. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the palace glow over your shoulder. The streets are narrow, so you may only get part of the building in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the southern start of Rue Droite, where the street runs down towards the sea, while you stand by the palace at number 15.
card.rules_and_safety: The streets are public, but the museum inside is a separate visit, so check the official site before you go to see what you can photograph.
card.challenge: Find the cannonball, then get it low in the frame with the lit palace glowing behind it. Bonus points if the walls stay straight.
card.good_to_know: The Palais Lascaris is a 17th-century town house. The Vintimille-Lascaris family owned it until 1802, and the city bought it in 1942. Restoration ran from 1962 to 1970, and today it's a museum of historic musical instruments with over 500 pieces.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Rue de la Loge at the corner on the palace's edge, where the cannonball is set into the stonework. Face the lit-up palace, which you'll see at an angle.

card.hook: Walk up Avenue Nicolas II and the green and gold onion domes pop into view before you've even looked for them. This one is easy: the building does all the work.
card.stand_here: Stand on Avenue Nicolas II, near the cathedral entrance, and face north. The front of the cathedral is straight ahead, with its domes and colourful brickwork.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole façade. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the domes and brickwork. Use 0.5x only if you move close to the entrance and want the whole building in the frame.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the façade, then slide it a touch darker so the gold stays rich and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Late morning to afternoon is best. One guide says that's when the colours look brightest.
card.selfie_here: Head to the green garden behind the cathedral, near the marble bust of Grand Duke Nicolas Alexandrovich. Use the front camera at 0.5x and turn so the domes rise over your shoulder, with the palm trees beside you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on Avenue Nicolas II, where the domes come into view, to face the façade while you stand a little way ahead of them, towards the cathedral.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an active church, so keep your photos to the outside and don't point your phone at worshippers. Photography is not allowed inside.
card.challenge: Take one photo of the whole façade, then one of just the brickwork. Can a friend guess it's the same building?
card.good_to_know: The cathedral opened in 1912 and was consecrated that December, in memory of Tsarevich Nicholas Alexandrovich, who died in Nice. Tsar Nicholas II paid for the building work. It's a national monument of France and is described as the largest Eastern Orthodox cathedral in Western Europe.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Avenue Nicolas II, near the cathedral entrance, and face north. The front of the cathedral is straight ahead, with its domes and colourful brickwork.

selfie_spots.why: The leafy garden with palm trees gives a calm, Riviera-style backdrop that sets the cathedral's onion domes apart from the rest of Nice.

card.hook: Picture a big white square arch standing on four legs, stepping right over the course of the Paillon. That's MAMAC, and honestly the building is as good a photo as anything inside it.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, on the Niki de Saint Phalle esplanade above Place Yves Klein, right at the building. Face the museum and step back until the whole white block fits.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the whole building and its arch fit, since you're standing close. Then switch to 1x for a more natural look, and try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for marble edges and upper-level details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the vertical edges straight, then tap the brightest white wall and slide darker a touch so the marble stays white instead of going grey.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day when the sun is on the facade, so the marble pops against blue sky. Early morning or late afternoon gives softer shadows.
card.selfie_here: Try the Esplanade Niki de Saint Phalle, in front of the museum entrance, overlooking Place Yves Klein. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep MAMAC's white walls behind you over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to take your photo from the square near the museum, Place Garibaldi, so the arch and white marble facade frame you while you stand on the esplanade.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official site before you go for current opening days and any photography rules. If you go inside, check the photo rules at the desk first.
card.challenge: Find the most perfectly straight white corner you can, fill the whole frame with marble and shadow, and see if your gridlines agree it's straight.
card.good_to_know: MAMAC opened on 21 June 1990 and was designed by Yves Bayard and Henri Vidal. The facades are covered in smooth white Carrara marble. Inside, there are about 4,500 square metres over ten showrooms.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, on the Niki de Saint Phalle esplanade above Place Yves Klein, right at the building. Face the museum and step back until the whole white block fits.

card.hook: Picture a busy shopping street, scooters and shoppers everywhere, and then a huge Gothic church front rising at the far end like it wandered in from another century. That's your photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on the stretch of Avenue Jean Médecin that faces the front of Notre-Dame de Nice, and face the basilica so the two towers sit at the end of the avenue. Shoppers and shop fronts in the foreground are a bonus, not a problem.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the towers and the street together. If you're close and can't fit both towers in, drop to zoom 0.5x. For the rose window and the tops of the towers, try zoom 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the two towers up with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean, and leave a little space above the towers so they don't get chopped off.
card.best_time: Pick a time when the front is evenly lit and the pavement isn't too packed. If people are in the way, wait a moment for a gap, or keep them in the shot for scale and life.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and switch to zoom 0.5x so more of the building squeezes in. Step back from the church and put the towers over your shoulder, with the avenue behind you for a bit of everyday Nice.
card.rules_and_safety: Be careful taking photos in the city centre. One reviewer says the best shots are from the tram tracks, but the exact spot isn't confirmed, so don't stand on the tracks. The basilica is a place of worship with its own opening times, so check the official site if you want to go inside, and skip the flash if you do.
card.challenge: Take two shots from the same spot: one with a clear gap in the pedestrians, and one packed with people. Which one feels more like Nice?
card.good_to_know: Notre-Dame de Nice is the largest church in the city, but it isn't the cathedral. It was built between 1864 and 1868 to a design by Louis Lenormand. The neo-Gothic style was chosen on purpose: Nice had just passed from the Kingdom of Sardinia to France, and Gothic was then seen as typically French. The two square towers are each 65 m high, with a big rose window between them.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the stretch of Avenue Jean Médecin that faces the front of Notre-Dame de Nice, and face the basilica so the two towers sit at the end of the avenue. Shoppers and shop fronts in the foreground are a bonus, not a problem.

The only named photo position is the tram tracks, which comes from a single reviewer's comment, not a guide. The basilica is on Avenue Jean Médecin (Tripadvisor, Nice tourist office, Seenice). Photography is permitted without flash, and visitors should avoid flash (audiala.com and airial.travel), but no page mentions selfie sticks or tripods, so no such rule is listed.

card.hook: Nice's Old Town is all narrow lanes and tall shutters, and then a Baroque church pops out of the jumble like it's been squeezed in with a shoehorn. A 42-metre brick bell tower rises right behind it, and that much exposed brick is rare in Nice.
card.stand_here: Stand in Place du Jésus, on the parvis right in front of the façade, and face the church. The square is small, so back up to the far side to fit the whole front in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x, because you can't step back far and it squeezes in the façade and the tower. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the bell tower or the top of the façade.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the façade up with the vertical lines, keeping your phone level so the walls don't lean in.
card.best_time: Go early in the day if you can. The square is likely to be quieter, so it's easier to get the church without strangers wandering through.
card.selfie_here: Take it in Place du Jésus, on the square facing the church, with the façade behind you. The Restaurant du Gésu across from the church is a handy landmark to check you're in the right spot. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and tilt up a little so the church fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the small placette on rue Droite and take a short step back to fit the whole façade, while you pose in front of the church.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working church, so be discreet. Check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and any rules on photography inside.
card.challenge: Look up and find the Ligurian tiles around the base of the dome, then zoom in and see how much texture you can catch.
card.good_to_know: The Jesuits settled in Nice in 1603 and began this church in 1642. The main building was finished in 1650, but the Baroque façade you see today only came in 1825. It's been a listed historical monument since 1971, and inside, the vault shows scenes from the life of Saint Jacques le Majeur.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Place du Jésus, on the parvis right in front of the façade, and face the church. The square is small, so back up to the far side to fit the whole front in.

selfie_research.notes: The Place du Jésus and rue Droite placette spots are named on the pages, but none of the pages gives explicit selfie advice; the 'best selfie' choice is my inference from the descriptions. The ask-someone spot is the same placette as the second selfie spot, and the source describes it as a photo spot for the facade rather than a passer-by position. The Wikimedia photo dates from 2006. No page I found states rules on selfie sticks or tripods, so none are reported. Church photo rules, which are not selfie-stick or tripod rules, appear on a Nice church page: photography is generally allowed inside for personal use, without flash and discreetly during services (airial.travel Église du Gesù page). No safety point was found on any page.
